reasoning: This is a narrative review article discussing clinical presentation, aetiology, pathophysiology, and treatments of cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. It synthesizes existing literature without generating new software or new research data, nor does it analyze a specific existing dataset. No research software or data is created or substantively used.

This is a clinical consensus guideline paper based on expert review of existing literature and systematic reviews. It does not involve creation or use of research software, nor does it generate or analyze new research data - it synthesizes existing published evidence into clinical recommendations.

The study uses an existing research software tool (TopoToolbox V2) to process DEM data and delineate stream networks/catchments, but does not develop or extend new software. However, the research generates a new national-scale geodatabase of catchment and morphometric characteristics for 128 Philippine river catchments, which is a substantive new dataset created through the research (derived from DEM analysis) and made accessible via a web app. This constitutes generation of new research data, while the software (TopoToolbox) is used rather than created.

The paper develops a new visualization tool/software that applies the Jaya algorithm (with Latin Hypercube Sampling enhancement) to graph drawing, representing newly created research software used to generate novel results (S1). It also generates synthetic graph datasets using the Erdős–Rényi model for benchmarking, in addition to using some real-world datasets, creating new data specifically for this research's experiments (D1).

This is a study protocol for a planned randomised clinical trial. It describes future recruitment, interventions, and outcome assessments but does not report any actual data collection, analysis, or software development/use. As per the rules, protocols describing planned work without evidence of actual data/software generation or use should be classified as S3D3.

This study generated new research data through surveys (n=153 nurses/midwives across four cohorts), semi-structured interviews, and thematic analysis to measure confidence/importance scores on genomics competencies. This is primary data collection generating novel survey/interview data, hence D1. There is no indication of research software being created or used for analysis beyond standard statistical/survey tools (e.g., basic statistics for Likert scale scoring), which are utility tools rather than research software contributing new knowledge, so S3.

The paper appears to be an editorial/introduction to a special issue on machine learning and deep learning applications in finance, education, and healthcare, with no abstract content provided beyond the title and bibliographic details. There is no evidence of new software or data being generated or used within this specific paper itself—it is likely a summary/overview piece rather than original empirical research. Without concrete evidence of software or dataset creation/use described in the text, it defaults to S3D3.

The study used existing imaging/treatment planning software and TCP models (not newly developed software) to process DW-MRI data from 10 GBM patients, generating new patient-specific ADC-derived cellular density maps, TCP maps, and dose escalation plans—constituting newly generated research data. No new software tool was created; existing analysis/planning tools were applied to derive novel in-silico results, so it is Software Used (S2) and Data Generated (D1).

This is a translational pathology study that generated new research data (multiplexed immunofluorescence immune cell phenotyping data from NLPHL and THRLBCL patient tissue samples), creating new knowledge about immune cell composition across histological subtypes. The study used existing research software (image analysis/multiplexed immunofluorescence quantification platforms) as a tool to analyse the tissue samples, rather than developing new software. Hence the data is generated (D1) while software is merely used as a utility (S2).

The study collected original survey data (384 startup directors/representatives) using BRCS, MBI-GS, and a custom COVID-19 stress questionnaire, generating a new dataset for burnout prediction - this constitutes new research data (D1). For analysis, they used a GMDH neural network, which is an existing computational/statistical method/technique applied to the data rather than a novel software tool created by the researchers; there's no indication they built or substantially extended new software, just used GMDH as an analytical technique/tool to generate findings, fitting S2 (software used to generate new knowledge).

The study generates new experimental research data: a novel crystal structure of AMG-176 bound to Mcl-1 and NMR-based conformer analysis data for the inhibitors, which are new findings central to the paper's conclusions. There is no mention of developing or significantly extending any research software; standard crystallography/NMR processing tools would be used as utilities rather than being a focus of the research or generating new knowledge themselves.

This is a cluster RCT generating new primary data through assessments of mothers/children over multiple time points (pregnancy, 3, 6, 15, 24 months) across 8 clinics. This data collection is substantive and central to the research findings. There is no mention of developing or using specialized research software; standard statistical analysis tools would be utility software, not research software generating new knowledge.

The study uses existing electronic health record datasets (UK Biobank primary care data and CPRD GOLD) linked to cancer registry data to develop symptom/test phenotypes and analyse pre-diagnosis consultation rates. While new phenotypes (code lists) are constructed, these are analytic definitions applied to existing EHR data rather than newly generated research data in the sense of new datasets; the underlying substantive data used (UK Biobank, CPRD) is pre-existing. No new research software is created or substantially extended—statistical analyses were performed using standard Poisson regression models, likely via standard statistical software used as a utility, not a novel research software artifact. Thus this is S3 (no software generated/used beyond standard tools) and D2 (existing data used, generating new knowledge through analysis).

This is a perspective/opinion piece discussing decolonisation of the psychology curriculum. It does not report any empirical study involving software development or use, nor does it generate or use any research data (datasets, corpora, etc.). It is purely a conceptual/argumentative discussion, so it falls under No Software, No Data.

This is a Scientific Data descriptor paper that compiles and presents a novel global dataset (DOCU-CLIM) of 621 documentary climate time series, including previously unpublished series, generating new substantive research data. The paper's primary contribution is the dataset itself, not new software - any analysis tools (proxy forward models, correlation analyses) are used as standard utilities rather than novel research software being developed/extended. Thus it falls under S3 (no research software generated/used for new knowledge) and D1 (research data generated).

The study develops a novel conceptual framework/explainable network model with multimodal learning (AI software) specifically to link biodiversity and abiotic data, which is a new computational tool applied to generate new knowledge - this constitutes research software generation. Additionally, the researchers generated new data through multilocus metabarcoding of lake sediment cores spanning 100 years, combined with newly measured biocide concentrations and climate records, creating a novel long-term biodiversity and environmental dataset. Both the software (AI/network modeling framework) and data (metabarcoding, biocide, climate time series) were generated as part of this research to produce new findings about freshwater biodiversity change.

This is a state-of-the-art review article summarizing existing literature on blood-brain barrier imaging techniques. It does not generate or use any specific research software, nor does it create or analyze a novel dataset. It synthesizes prior findings and discusses future directions without reporting new empirical data collection or software development/use for analysis.

This is a cross-sectional survey study where the researchers collected primary data from 10,007 respondents via questionnaires on COVID-19 knowledge, vaccine willingness, and uptake. This constitutes generation of new research data (D1). Statistical analyses (linear regression, logistic regression, GSEM) were performed, likely using standard statistical software (e.g., Stata or similar), but no new research software was created or significantly extended; the tools used are standard statistical utilities rather than research software generating new knowledge themselves (S3).

This is a review article discussing concepts and challenges in post-GWAS interpretation of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease genetic risk. It does not report generation or use of specific software tools or datasets as part of original research; rather it synthesizes existing literature, discussing general computational tools and genomic datasets in the field without creating new software or data, nor substantively using specific existing datasets/software for new analysis.

This is a narrative literature review summarizing existing knowledge on MAIT cells and the microbiome. It does not report generation or use of any specific research software, nor does it generate or analyze new research data/datasets; it synthesizes findings from prior studies without new experimental or computational work.

The researchers created a novel counterfactual GAN architecture specifically for this study, which represents newly generated research software that enables the generation of counterfactual OCT images and new scientific insight into retinal aging. This qualifies as S1 (Software Generated). For data, they used the existing UK Biobank OCT imaging dataset (85,709 adults) as their primary research data source, rather than generating a new dataset themselves - the UK Biobank data was collected as part of a separate population study and used here for analysis, making this D2 (Data Used).

The researchers used an existing pretrained generative language model (GPT-2) and existing NLP embedding tools as software utilities to generate novel simulated data—FTD-like narratives under different parameter manipulations (stochasticity, memory span). This simulated narrative data is newly generated research data used to test theoretical hypotheses about thought disorder measures, constituting new substantive data. The software itself (GPT-2) was not created or substantially modified by the researchers; it was used as a tool, and a Python tutorial accompanies the paper, but this is documentation rather than new research software. Thus, software is used (not generated) and data (simulated narratives) is generated by the research.

This is a study protocol describing a planned cross-sectional survey. No actual software was developed (Qualtrics is used as a utility tool for survey distribution, not research software generating new knowledge), and no data has yet been collected or analyzed - the paper describes future data collection plans. As per the criteria, planned/proposed artefacts are not considered evidence of generation or use, so this protocol paper is classified as S3D3.

This paper reports phase 1 clinical trials (crossover studies) generating new pharmacokinetic data (Cmax, AUC values) from healthy subjects on drug-drug interactions with rezafungin. This is newly generated clinical/experimental research data, classifying as D1. There is no mention of any research software being created or used to generate new knowledge - standard statistical analysis tools would have been used as utilities only, not as a focus of the research, so S3 applies.

The paper uses existing UK Biobank data (anthropometric, physical activity, dietary data) and existing scoring methodology, but through the operationalisation process generates a new derived dataset: adherence scores for the WCRF/AICR recommendations for 158,415 and 314,616 participants. This derived score dataset is a new research data product that didn't exist before, so it counts as data generated (D1). No new software tool is described as being created or substantively used to generate new knowledge beyond routine calculation; the scoring is a methodological framework, not software development, so S3.

This is a literature review discussing cardiovascular risk prediction methods, biomarkers, and ocular imaging approaches. It does not report any new software development or use of existing research software to generate results, nor does it generate or use a specific research dataset; it synthesizes existing literature and identifies research gaps. Hence it falls under no software and no data.

The study uses Google Trends (an existing tool/data source) and Joinpoint regression software (existing statistical software, NCI's Joinpoint program) to analyze pre-existing Google search data. No new software was created; the Joinpoint software is an existing analytical tool used to generate new knowledge (trend analysis), classifying as S2. The Google Trends search volume data is existing, publicly available data (not generated by the researchers) but substantively used to produce new findings about mpox information-seeking behavior, classifying as D2.

This qualitative study collected original interview data from 30 Dental Officers and 17 Dental Managers via semi-structured interviews, generating new primary research data (thematic analysis data) specific to this study - qualifying as D1 (Data Generated). The analysis was done through manual thematic analysis rather than specialized research software, so no research software was created or substantively used to generate new knowledge (S3 - No Research Software).

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis that synthesizes data extracted from 76 articles and two national surveys to compute new pooled prevalence estimates (stunting, thinness, overweight/obesity, micronutrient deficiencies). This extraction and synthesis constitutes generation of new research data (meta-analytic dataset) producing new knowledge not present in any single source study. No research software was created or substantively used to generate new knowledge; standard statistical tools (e.g., meta-analysis software) would be used only as routine utilities, not described as novel or integral methodological contributions.

The study generated new experimental data by recording high-density surface EMG from children with DCD and typically developing children, and decomposing signals into motor unit action potential trains - this is newly collected research data specific to this study (D1). The decomposition and analysis likely used existing EMG decomposition software/algorithms (e.g., standard HDsEMG decomposition tools) rather than developing new software, so software was used as a utility/tool to generate new knowledge from the data, fitting S2 (existing research software used to enable analysis) rather than S1 (no claim of creating new software) or S3 (the decomposition software is more than a trivial utility, it's central to deriving motor unit characteristics but there's no clear evidence of novel software being developed in this paper).
